title: Not even "uff"
hook: don't say even uff to your parents, and lower the wing of humility to them (17:23–24)

segments.voice: Yesterday, by night: the journey from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque. Your line was taken by night. Did a dark stretch show you anything? Day four hundred fifty-eight.

Your mother asks you, for the third time this week, how to send a photo on her phone. You show her. And somewhere in the showing, before you've decided to, a small sound escapes: a breath out through the nose, a tiny sigh. It's a small sound that means: this again. In Arabic it's uff. And Surah seventeen, in a passage of commands about how to live, names that exact sound and rules it out.

The passage begins: your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and kindness to parents. Notice the order. Right after God come the people who raised you. Then the scene narrows to old age, when one or both of them live with you and need you. In Pickthall's translation: "say not 'Fie' unto them nor repulse them, but speak unto them a gracious word." Fie is his old English for uff. Commentators make the point that uff is about the smallest sound of annoyance there is. If the smallest is ruled out, everything bigger is too. Then verse twenty-four gives a picture: lower to them the wing of humility, out of mercy. The picture is a bird lowering its wings over its chicks. Once, your parents did that for you. Now the wings are yours, and you lower them over the people who once covered you. And the verse gives words to say: "My Lord! Have mercy on them both as they did care for me when I was little." The name for all this is birr al-walidayn. Birr is a wide word, goodness, devotion, dutiful kindness. Walidayn means the two parents. A hadith in Bukhari tells of a man who asked the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ who most deserves his good company. Your mother, he said. Then who? Your mother. Then who? Your mother. Then who? Your father. The verse doesn't say parents are always right. Another verse, 31:15, says not to obey parents who push you to set partners beside God, and still to keep company with them kindly in this world. Gentleness even then, and it begins with the smallest sound.
screen: `GOD FIRST, THEN PARENTS.` · `NOT EVEN UFF.` · `THE WING LOWERED IN MERCY.` · `YOUR MOTHER, THREE TIMES.` · then, large: `SPEAK UNTO THEM A GRACIOUS WORD.`

segments.voice: Sit, and bring one parent to mind. Or someone who did a parent's work for you: a grandparent, an aunt, a foster parent. If they've died, this is for them too. Remember one ordinary thing they did for you when you were small: a lunch packed, a ride home, a hand on your forehead. Hold it. If you pray, you can say the verse's own words for them: my Lord, have mercy on them both as they cared for me when I was little. If they're living, choose one thing to do for them this week. The bell holds the time.
Birr al-walidayn. Goodness to the two parents, placed right after the worship of God, down to the smallest sigh. Today's word.
Your line: not even a sigh. Today, the next time an older person asks you something for the third time, answer as if it were the first. Day four hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: Muslims treat kindness to parents as a major duty, especially in their old age; the prayer of 17:24 is often said for parents after the daily prayers, and keep praying for them after they die.

match.prompt: inside the verses — tap the pairs.

myth: the verse comes right after the command to worship God alone
17:23 joins the two: worship none but Him, and kindness to parents.
birr al-walidayn means obeying parents even in wrongdoing
31:15: don't obey them in wrongdoing against God, yet keep company with them kindly.
in Bukhari's hadith, the father is named first
the mother is named three times, then the father.

fork.setup: a man asks the Prophet who most deserves his good company. the Prophet says: your mother. then who?
fork.reveal: your mother, again, and a third time, and only then your father (Bukhari).

original.note: Arabic: goodness to the two parents. walidayn is the dual: both parents.

trapdoor: what you thought: be respectful to your parents.
what it means: right after worshiping God, kindness to parents, down to not letting out a sigh, and lowering the wing of mercy to them.
what a scholar hears: commentators note uff is the slightest sound of displeasure, so anything larger is ruled out a fortiori; 'janah adh-dhull' is a bird's wing lowered.

notes: Pickthall wording of 17:23 and 17:24 quoted from memory; confirm exactly. Pickthall prints Fie in double quotation marks; single marks used here inside the quotation.
Bukhari 5971 number cited from memory; confirm.
The practice offers the Qur'anic prayer of 17:24 to those who pray; confirm suitability for parents who are not Muslim (scholars discuss this).
'Scholars agree you don't obey a parent in wrongdoing' rests on 29:8 and 31:15 and the hadith 'no obedience in disobedience'; confirm wording.
